(3) Whether the decision of the reviewing authority, namely the Government of Bangladesh can be called in question under Article 102 of the Constitution despite the Proclamation of 6.4.79", 

 7. As required under clause (2) of Regulation 4 of martial Law Regulation No. 1 of 1975 the proceedings after termination were submitted to the Government for review and the result of the review was communicated on August 29, 1978. In the communication an extract taken from the order of review was incorporated it states, inter alia, that the review does not disclose any point of fact or law which would warrant disturbance of the sentence. Thereafter the case was submitted before the President for confirmation. The President confirmed the death sentence on September 21, 1978. After confirmation of the sentence by the President the appellant filed a petition under sections 401 and 402 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to the Government with a prayer to remit the sentence as whole or commute the same. This petition was rejected and she result was communicated by the letter dated June 8, 1979, which was received on June 10, 1979. Before communication of the order of rejection of the petition Martial Law was lifted by the Proclamation dated April 6, 1979. Thereafter the writ petition was moved on June 11, 1979 which was rejected on June 12, 1979 after hearing the Attorney-General of the Government of Bangladesh. 

 12. Mr. M. H. Khondker next submitted dames (6) of Regulation 4 provides that subject to review, all orders, judgment and sentence of Martial Law Court shall be final. He argued that in this case there was no revile as contemplated under the Regulation. According to him, the review should have been made by the re viewing authority as contemplated under the Regulation, that is, as the substitute of appellant authority. It may be mentioned that by amendment review by the Government was substituted for appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Clause (4) of Regulation 4 provides that the Government may, on review, so aside vary or modify any order, Judgment or sentence or make orders for retrial or such other orders as it deems necessary for ends of justice. Clause (4) gives very wide power to the Government to review the case on termination of the Proceedings before the Martial Law Court. With reference to the expression for ends of Justice" the karate C tinsel submitted that existence of this expression sufficiently indicates the scone of the power of the reviewing authority. He submitted that in the instance case as per information received from the Ministry of Law there was no proper review as contemplated under the n which is indicated oat the Memo, dated September  23,1978 from the Ministry of Law enclosing an extract of the review note. The memorandum annexed to the writ petition as annexure 'D reads as under:- 

 14. To verify the factual position, reference to the office file became necessary. The learned Attorney-General being ready with the relevant file in respect of review by the Government and confirmation of the sentence by the President produced the same before the Court for examination. Annexure 'D' contains the reference of the File No. JIV-Con-150/78 Ministry of Law, Justice Branch, Section-IV. The file contains an elaborate note of review. The note is so elaborate and contains full discussion on point of fact and law it could very well be termed as a well-written judgment by a Court. The learned Counsel of the appellant was allowed by the Court to check up himself as to whether the statement made in the writ petition and also In the Special Leave Petition are justified. On finding the note the learned Counsel found it difficult to press the point further. He, however, attempted to make some comments none of which can be treated as relevant or justified. The review note as contained in the file practically took much wind out of the sail, that is, the main ground of attack against the confirmation of the sentence by the President lost its force. 

 19. With the above observation the Court repelled the arguments advanced in support of the view that the Constitution as such was still in force as the supreme law of the country, untrammelled by the Proclamation and Martial Lew Regulation. In this context much reliance was placed by Mr. M. H. Khondker on the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Asma Jilani vs. Government of Panjab, P.L.D. 1972 (S.C.) 139, to which reference will be made later on. 

 23. Now let me examine whether Asma Jilani's case upon which much reliance has been placed by Mr. M.H. Khondker lends any real support to the contentions raised by him. On carefully going through the decision in Asma Jilani’s case it appears that the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of Pakistan bathe not followed the view taken in the case of State vs. Dosso (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 1; PLD 1958 (S.C) 533. The precise question before she Supreme Court was whether the High Courts have jurisdiction under Article 98 of the Constitution of Pakistan 1962 to enquire into the validity of detention under Martial Law Regulation No. 78 of 1971 in view of the bar created by the provisions of the Jurisdiction of Courts (Removal of Doubts) Order, 1969 and the further question was whether the doctrine enunciated in the case of State vs. Dosso was correct. So far as the second question is concerned the teamed Judges have taken the view that the principles laid down in Dosso's case that "where a Constitution and one national legal order under it is disrupted by an abrupt political change not within the contemplation of the Constitution then such a change is a revolution and its legal effect is not only the destruction of the Constitution but also the validity of the motorist legal order, irrespective of how or by whom such a change is brought about", are wholly unsustainable and cannot be treated as good law either on the principle of state decals or otherwise. In deciding the question of supremacy or the Consultation vis-a-vis the power of the Chief Martial Law Administrator according to the learned Judges, the decision in Dosso's case is not based upon correct enunciation of the principles of International Law attributed to Hans Kelsen's theory. They have commented that the doctrine enunciated by Hans Keisen was not only misapplied in Dosso's case but also the decision proceeded on the erroneous assumption that his doctrine was the generally accepted doctrine of the Modern Jurisprudence, Incidentally, it may be mentioned that the principal question agitated in Dosso's case as whether the proceedings which were for a writ of Habeas Corpus and /or Certiorari had abated by reason of the provision of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958. The question was answered in the affirmative. But when giving reasons for the decision, Muhammad Munir, C. J. who delivered the judgment, accorded legal recognition to the Martial Law itself by describing it as a successful revolution and, therefore, the proper, jaw creating agency. For proper appreciation of the decision Article 2 of the Law (Continuance in Force) Order, 1958 Is reproduced as under:— 

 24. In Dosso's case after elaborate discussion of the Constitutional provisions as being -kept operative by the Laws (Continuance in Force) Older, 1958 and the different provisions of the said Omer the Court held that by reason of the provisions of clauses (5) and (7) of Article 2 those writs hart abated. From the different clauses of Article 2 it appears that there was no total ouster of the jurisdiction of Ma Superior Courts power in issuing writs, and the only bar put under clause (5) was that no writ shall be issued against the Chief Administrator of Martial Law or the Deputy Chief Martial Law Administrator, or any person exercising power or jurisdiction under the authority of either. In Asma "Jilani’s case the learned Judges expressed the view that General Agha Mohammad Yahya Khan did not validly succeed to the power of the President on the authority of the miter dated March 24, 1969 from Field Marshal Mohammad Ayub Khan to the Commander-in-Chief of the Army. This handing over of power and subsequent Proclamation of Martial Law by General Mohammad Yahya Khan on March 25, 1969. Throughout Pakistan and assumption of the powers of the Chief Martial Law Administrator was wholly unauthorized. The learned Judges have held that the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces bad no power to abrogate the fundamental law of the country. As a normal conclusion they further held that the power of the Superior Courts remained untrammeled to issue an appropriate writ on making proper declaration. 

 27. Asma Jilani's case and Zia-ur-Rahman's case were reviewed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Federation of Pakistan vs, Saeed Ahmad, P L. D. 1974 (S.0 ) 151. A large number of writ petitions were filed in the High Courts under article 201 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1972 challenging the orders passed by the Government under the Removal from Service (Special Provision) Regulation (Martial Law Regulations No. 58 of 1969 and 114 of 1972). The Government took a preliminary objection as to the jurisdiction of the High Court to entertain the writ petitions The High Court took the view that notwithstanding the amendments made in clause (2) of Article 281 of the Interim Constitution of Pakistan tit the constitution (Sixth Amendment) Order, 1973 (President's Order No. 3 o 1973), no change had taken piece in the jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 201 of the said Constitution to examine cases to the limited extent that the action purported to have been taken were without jurisdiction or coram non judice and or mala fide actions. Then the Government took the mater to the Supreme Court contending, on the authority of Zia-ur-Rahman case, that she validity of the Martial Law. Regulations could not be called in question for the reasons given in the said judgment, It was further contended that as regards action taken under the said Martial Law Regulation, which was sought to be protected by clause (2) of Article 281 of the Interim Constitution, the intention of the law giver was that they should be fully protected from scrutiny by Court including the Supreme Court and the High Court, According to the Government, the ouster of the Jurisdiction is complete and the Court cannot eon any ground whatsoever call in question such actions, notwithstanding the judgments in the cases of Asma lama and Zia-ur-Rahman. Hamoodur Rahman, C. J. in repelling the Government's contention expressed the view that notwithstanding the ouster provision, the acts, orders, or proceedings, which are taken ox made without jurisdiction, mala fide or coram  non-judice, have not been saved from the scrutiny of the Courts by the ouster clause. I do not consider it necessary to dilate further on this question, particularly, in view of the fact that the proceedings either before the Special Martial Law Court or before the reviewing authority has not been challenged on any such around. So far as the proceedings before the Martial Law Court is concerned excepting the attack on the ground that whole proceedings became without jurisdiction in view of unauthorized transfer of the case, the learned Counsel had no comments to make. I have already noted that transfer was made by the Chief Martial Law Administrator himself and not by any delegate. Even the proceedings before the reviewing authority was not attacked excepting on the ground that it was not properly done as contemplated under Regulation 4(2) and (4) of Martial Law Regulation No. 1 of 1975. It has already been noticed that this grievance cannot stand in view of the elaborate decision given by the reviewing authority. In that view of the matter I do not consider any useful purpose would be melted by any discussion on the following cases, namely, Patterson vs. District Commissioner of Accra (1948) A.C. 341, Franklin vs. Minister of Town and Country Planning (1948) A.C. 87. Padfield vs. Minister of Agriculture etc. (1968) 1 All E.R. 694. 

 34. Mr. M. H. Khondker wanted to submit with reference to the petition under section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the report submitted by the Chairman of the Special Martial Law Court No. II recommending commutation of sentence of death to transportation that in view of the fact that the decision of the Martial Law Court was not unanimous and recommendation was made by the Chairman for commutation of sentence to transportation, it was incumbent upon the President to accept the recommendation and at least commute the sentence as per recommendation. From the file it appears that the Chairman of the Martial Law Court No. II recommended for alternation of sentence to transportation, but the power to suspend or remit sentences being absolutely within the discretion of the Government or the President, the Court has got no say in the matter. There may be very good reason for commuting the sentence by the confirming authority but there cannot be any direction from the Court for acceptance of the recommendation of the Court which passed the sentence of death. 

 38. The occurrence took place on 18.4.78 and the First Information Report was lodged on 20.4.78. Police submitted charge-sheet on 6 5.78. in the Court of Magistrate, 1st Class. Thereafter on 20.5.78, in pursuance of a notification by the Chief Martial Law Administrator, the case was transferred to the Special Martial Law Court. The appellant was convicted by the Martial Law Court on 5.8.78 and the Government upon review of the case placed the case before the President for confirmation of the death sentence which NM confirmed on 21.9.78 it appears that a mercy petition was filed by the appellant on 27.9.78 under sections 401 and 402 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and a report was called for from the Presiding Judge of the trial Court under section 401(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 16.10.78 and the Presiding Judge submitted report recommending commutation of she sentence on 21.10.78. Martial Law was lifted on 6.4 79. The appellant's father was intimated on 8.6.79 that the mercy petition had been dismissed. Thereafter the writ petition was filed before the High Court Division challenging the order of conviction and sentence passed by the Special Martial Law Court and for declaration that the confirmation of the death sentence had been made without lawful authority. The High Court Division though summarily rejects tad the wait petition after hearing both the sides holding that jurisdiction of the Court had been ousted by the Martial Law Proclamation yet had, in fact, dealt with case on merit. Is considered the argument that the review proceeding had not been disposed of according to law. It further considered that cognizance was not taken by the Sub-Divisional Officer and, therefore, the case was not pending for enquiry. Teen it considered that the transfer was not validly done. Again the High Court Division considered the contention that the equality before law and equal protection of law had been violated. It considered farther that the confirmation was not done by the proper authority. Having considered each of these contentions the High Court Division rejected them, and then considered that the jurisdiction of the Court is itself ousted by Martial Law Proclamation and as a result the petition was rejected summarily by observing;— 

 41. The transfer was done by the Chief Martial Law Administrator, whereas, in the case of Hail Joynal Abedin it was done by the Government as the law stood then Therefore, the question of supplying guideline to the executive achieved some importance in view of the argument that basis for arbitrary exercise of power has been laid by such a wide conferment of power without supplying any guideline. In the present case the Chief Martial Law Administrator himself has transferred the case and since this power has been conferred upon him, the question of guideline would not be relevant. He himself has passed the law and then acted under it No exception can be taken to such an order bee cause the orders not in excess of the power, Whether such power of transfer may operate In discriminatory manner need not be decided In this case and that it will be decided In an appropriate case. 

 44. Martial Law Regulation requires that upon termination of the proceeding the entire case be submitted to the Government for review and this power of review had been substituted in case of an appeal which was given previously, In review the Government can vary, modify or set aside or direct for retrial or pass any orders for ends of justice, It Is essentially a judicial act and strong expression has been used i.e. "ends of justice" This judicial act is to be performed by the executive no doubt and if there Is any lapse or if the review is not done in accordance with law, them Jurisdiction of the High Court Division be attracted. But in this case we have gone through the twenty-nine pages of the review note and we are fully satisfied that the review was done fairly and justly, 

 45. Lastly, as for the mere petition under sections 401 and 402 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, it is correct that this is the prerogative of the Government. Under section 402A this power has also been conferred In a much wider form upon the President and Article 57 of the Constitution empowers the President to grant pardon in any case, The Court has nothing to do In this sphere. It is the prerogative of the President. However, it should be mentioned that the mercy petition was filed on 27-9-78 and the Presiding Judge of the trial Court submitted his report on 21.10.78 but the fate of this petition was communicated only on 8-6-79, in other words after nine months when the appellant languishing in a death cell expecting the fate of his mercy petition. Inordinate delay is a factor to be considered but this is not the rule of law and the Court has nothing to do with it. In the result, therefore, I agree that this appeal should be dismissed.
